"This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed
investing to full-service wealth management, all in one place. No matter your investing
goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab."
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. President Trump stumped for Texas
Republican Attorney General and Senate candidate Ken Paxton in San Antonio today.
"How many presidents have we had that is doing what he is doing for us? So Mr. President,
I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas. We
are going to win this race. God bless you."
Trump won Texas by almost 14 points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen in the
state as it has nationally. Earlier today, Trump said he has no regrets at all about
endorsing Paxton over incumbent Republican John Cornyn during this year's primary election.
Paxton is now locked in a close race with Democrat James Talarico in what's normally
the country's largest reliably Republican state.
The State Department says it has officially requested additional information from Russia
about the death of a lab worker amid fears of "pneumatic plague," but President Trump
is downplaying concerns that this could be linked to a bio-weapons program, as NPR's
Michelle Kellerman reports.
President Trump says the Russians have given "a little information" about the situation
in Irkutsk. He was asked whether this could have been the result of work on a bio-weapon.
"Well, we don't think so. We're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think
so. And if you listen to them, it's under control."
Russia's public health agency says the lab worker died of pneumonia and that it was not
related to her work at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Irkutsk. Michelle Kellerman and
PR News, the State Department.
The FCC is considering a request to loosen rules on political robocalls, including those
with AI-generated voices. Current federal law bans most robocalls to cell phones. A
conservative group called Club for Growth is seeking the change, arguing it could improve
voter communication and polling accuracy. Consumer advocacy groups warn the change could
lead to a surge of unwanted and misleading calls before the midterms.
The FBI says it foiled a planned mass shooting at one of the nation's largest shopping malls.
As Matt Sepic of Minnesota Public Radio reports, an 18-year-old Minneapolis area man is charged
with providing material support to a foreign terrorist organization.
Investigators say 18-year-old Shaktun Mohammed told an informant that he wanted to go to Somalia
to fight with the Islamic State, but couldn't afford to travel, so instead plotted to attack
the Mall of America. Minneapolis special agent in charge, Chris Dotson, says the FBI arrested
Mohammed on Tuesday after an undercover agent sold him a semi-automatic rifle.
He didn't just buy the rifle. He also bought 30 round magazines, four of them, and 200
live rounds to be used in this attack.
Dotson says Mohammed planned his attack for October 24, the day of a Hmong Arts Festival
at the Megha Mall. For NPR News, I'm Matt Sepic in Minneapolis.
After listening to NPR News from Washington.
The Democratic National Committee has sued the Trump administration over recent TV ads
promoting the president. The lawsuit claims the ads are government-sponsored propaganda
and asks a judge to block the use of federal funds to pay for them. The ads have cost taxpayers
at least $12 million. Trump says his super PAC will pay going forward.
The CDC is working with epidemiologists to create a new standard definition of a measles
death, and PR's Maria Godoy reports.
The Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists started work on a new definition of a measles
death earlier this year. Last month, the CDC announced it had joined the effort. The timing
raised eyebrows. It came after Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., a longtime vaccine
skeptic, questioned whether some of the five measles deaths reported by Pennsylvania were
really caused by the disease. Former CDC official Dr. Dimitri Daskalakis says he hopes the epidemiologist
group comes up with a definition that makes it harder to politicize measles deaths.
That definition, like the point of doing it is to remove ambiguity where it can't be weaponized.
The new definition is expected in two to three months. Maria Godoy, NPR News.
San Francisco 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk has won his appeal over nearly $30,000 in
fines issued by the NFL for what it deemed offensive celebrations when he imitated drinking
a beverage. The league said it looked like he was chugging a beer. Juszczyk says the
celebration is about drinking juice. That's a reference to his nickname. This is NPR.
This message comes from Charles Schwab with their original podcast Choiceology hosted by Katie Milkman,
an award-winning behavioral scientist and author of the best-selling book How to Change. Choiceology
is a show about the psychology and economics behind people's decisions. Hear true stories
from Nobel laureates, historians, authors, athletes, and more about why people do the
things they do. Download the latest episode and subscribe at Schwab.com/podcast or wherever
you listen.

Democratic National Committee sues Trump administration over government-funded TV ads promoting president
CDC works with epidemiologists to create new standard definition of measles death
